planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, gravelly or serpentine-derived soil in full sun; this low mat-former needs sharp drainage and a dry summer rest to perform well.

directions: Siskiyou mat is a ground-hugging evergreen shrub confined to open serpentine barrens and dry conifer forest of the Klamath-Siskiyou region of southwestern Oregon and northwestern California, where it forms sprawling woody mats a few inches tall but many feet wide. In spring it is studded with small clustered flowers in blue, lavender, or near-white, attracting native bees to otherwise sparse, rocky ground. Give it lean, fast-draining soil and full sun, and withhold summer water once roots are established, since the plant evolved under a strict winter-wet, summer-dry regime. It works well as a slow, tenacious groundcover for sunny rock gardens, slopes, or gravel beds that mimic its native barrens.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, mineral, serpentine-derived soil in full sun to light shade; this high-elevation Klamath-Siskiyou endemic needs a firm dry summer dormancy.

directions: Siskiyou fritillary is a diminutive bulb restricted to high serpentine talus slopes of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains at 3,000 to 6,700 feet, where exposed, nutrient-poor rock keeps competing vegetation sparse. Its short stems carry a few thick, sickle-shaped leaves and one or more nodding, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to purple tones with dense dark mottling. In cultivation it demands the same gritty, mineral soil and bone-dry summer dormancy it experiences in the wild, making it best suited to a bulb frame, scree bed, or alpine trough rather than an irrigated border. Source only nursery-propagated bulbs from a specialty bulb grower, since wild populations are small and easily disturbed.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in lean, gritty, serpentine-derived rocky soil in full sun; this dwarf native resents rich ground or summer irrigation.

directions: Siskiyou onion is a dwarf bulb endemic to the Klamath Mountains of southern Oregon and northern California, where it grows directly from serpentine and other rocky, mineral-poor soils on exposed slopes. A pair of narrow, curved leaves barely clears the ground before the plant sends up a short stalk topped with a dense, rounded cluster of dark-veined pink to lavender flowers in late spring to early summer. Because the whole plant stays only a few inches tall, it reads best in a scree bed, alpine trough, or raised rock garden where its dense flower heads can be viewed up close. Give it sharp drainage and a dry summer rest to match the winter-wet, summer-dry cycle of its native habitat.

planting.note: Sow seed outdoors in fall to early winter so it cold-stratifies naturally, or plant divisions into humus-rich, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade.

directions: Northern phlox trails along the forest floor of mixed-conifer and mixed-evergreen woodlands through the Klamath-Siskiyou region of southwestern Oregon and far northern California, with reclining mat-forming stems that turn upward into short flowering branches. In late spring it produces showy pink, five-lobed flowers with paler, almost white centers that stand out against the dim understory. Give it humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil and dappled shade similar to its native conifer-forest floor, and avoid soggy ground, which it tolerates far less well than full dryness between rains. It makes an attractive, low-growing companion for native ferns and trilliums in a shaded native-plant bed.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, mineral, serpentine-influenced soil in full sun to light shade; this Klamath-Siskiyou endemic needs a dry summer rest and resents heavy clay.

directions: Bolander's lily is a rare, highly localized lily of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains, confined to serpentine-derived soils in dry montane forest and chaparral of northwestern California and southwestern Oregon. Wiry stems carry up to nine nodding, bell-shaped flowers in red tones marked with yellow and purple, a color pattern that draws hummingbird pollinators rather than bees. Because wild populations depend on impeccable drainage and a long rainless summer, cultivated bulbs do best in a raised bed or scree garden where irrigation can be withheld once foliage yellows. Buy only nursery-propagated, virus-tested stock from a reputable native-bulb or rare-plant specialist rather than collecting from the wild.

planting.note: Plant rhizomatous bulbs in fall into constantly moist to boggy, serpentine-seep soil in partial shade; this streamside subspecies needs far more water than most garden lilies.

directions: Vollmer's lily is a subspecies of the widespread leopard lily restricted to serpentine seeps and watercourses of the Klamath-Siskiyou region in Del Norte County, California, and Josephine County, Oregon, often growing with its roots directly in running water. It differs from typical leopard lily in its unbranched rhizomes and carries the same reflexed, red-orange, dark-spotted flowers held above whorled leaves in summer. Unlike most native lilies that demand sharp drainage, this one wants consistently saturated, humus-rich soil, making it a natural fit for a bog garden, pond margin, or streamside planting rather than a dry rock garden. Give it partial shade and never let the root zone dry out through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into lean, rocky, serpentine or other ultramafic substrate in full sun to partial shade; good drainage is essential.

directions: Applegate stonecrop is a dusty blue-grey succulent confined almost entirely to the Applegate River watershed of the Klamath Mountains in southern Oregon and far northern California, colonizing bare rock outcrops and thin, rocky, often serpentine-derived soils. Its waxy rosettes multiply sideways into tight, lacy, snowflake-like clusters, and in summer send up short sprays of pale creamy-yellow starry flowers. Because it is adapted to extremely lean, mineral substrate with little organic matter, it performs best in a trough, raised scree bed, or crevice garden rather than ordinary garden soil, and resents being kept wet. Light afternoon shade in hot inland gardens helps preserve the rosettes' color and prevents scorching.

planting.note: Sow in fall so seed cold-stratifies naturally into lean, gritty, serpentine-derived rocky soil in full sun to light shade; mature plants resent rich soil and summer water.

directions: Siskiyou buckwheat forms low, woolly mats on rocky, often serpentine, substrate in the lower montane conifer forests of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains, typically well above 3,000 feet elevation. From summer into fall it sends up short stalks topped with tight, spherical clusters of bright yellow flowers that age to rusty tones, held just above the gray-woolly foliage. It is easier in cultivation than many serpentine specialists provided it has sharp drainage and lean, mineral soil, making it a good choice for a rock garden, scree bed, or trough at higher, cooler elevations. Avoid fertile soil and routine irrigation, both of which encourage floppy growth and shorten its life.
